title: Kubernetes Security in Depth
subtitle: Hardening, RBAC, admission policy, secrets and supply chain
description: Secure Kubernetes in layers: harden workloads, design least-privilege RBAC, enforce policy at admission, manage secrets safely and protect the software supply chain with signing, scanning and runtime detection.
outcomes: Harden pods with securityContext, seccomp and Pod Security Standards
Design and audit least-privilege RBAC and short-lived ServiceAccount tokens
Enforce rules with ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, Kyverno or Gatekeeper
Manage, encrypt and rotate secrets, and verify image signatures at admission

modules.title: Workload hardening and access control
modules.summary: Threat model, securityContext, Pod Security Standards and RBAC.

lessons.title: Threat model and workload hardening
lessons.summary: The 4Cs, what an attacker does after a foothold, and how securityContext, seccomp, AppArmor and Pod Security Standards stop it.
objectives: Apply the 4Cs model to decide where a control belongs
Harden a Pod with securityContext, seccomp and dropped capabilities
Enforce baseline and restricted Pod Security Standards per namespace

sections.title: Security is layers, not a switch
sections.body:
Kubernetes ships with permissive defaults: any pod can talk to any pod, containers run as whatever user the image says, and the default ServiceAccount token is mounted automatically. Securing a cluster means adding layers so that one mistake does not become a full compromise. The cloud-native model calls these layers the **4Cs**: **Cloud** (or datacenter), **Cluster**, **Container** and **Code**. Each layer builds on the security of the one below, and a weakness in an inner layer cannot be fixed by an outer one.

This course starts at the workload boundary, where most real incidents begin: a vulnerable application gets remote code execution inside a container, and the attacker then asks, what can I reach from here? Your job is to make the honest answer be: almost nothing. Typical attacker steps are: read the mounted ServiceAccount token, scan the pod network, query the node metadata service, break out through a privileged container or hostPath, and read Secrets from environment variables. Every control in this course cuts one of those steps.

sections.title: About this example: a hardened Pod manifest
sections.body: This is a complete Pod you can apply with `kubectl apply -f hardened-pod.yaml`. It runs as a fixed non-root UID, forbids privilege escalation, drops every Linux capability, makes the root filesystem read-only and opts into the runtime's default seccomp profile. Look at `securityContext` at both pod level and container level, and at the `emptyDir` mounted on `/tmp`, which gives the app a writable scratch area despite the read-only rootfs.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hardened-web
  namespace: secure-demo
  labels:
    app: hardened-web
spec:
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 10001
    runAsGroup: 10001
    fsGroup: 10001
    seccompProfile:
      type: RuntimeDefault
  containers:
    - name: web
      image: nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.27-alpine
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
      securityContext:
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
        capabilities:
          drop: ["ALL"]
      resources:
        requests: {cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi}
        limits: {memory: 128Mi}
      volumeMounts:
        - {name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp}
        - {name: cache, mountPath: /var/cache/nginx}
  volumes:
    - {name: tmp, emptyDir: {}}
    - {name: cache, emptyDir: {}}
sections.title: hardened-pod.yaml
sections.note: `automountServiceAccountToken: false` removes the API token from the pod entirely, which is the right default for a web server that never calls the API.

sections.title: About this example: verifying the hardening from inside the pod
sections.body: These commands apply the manifest above and then run `id`, a write test and a capability check inside the container. Run them after `kubectl apply` to prove that the settings are enforced and not just declared. The interesting lines are `uid=10001`, the `Read-only file system` error on `/etc` and the all-zero `CapEff` mask.

sections.code:
kubectl create namespace secure-demo
kubectl apply -f hardened-pod.yaml
kubectl -n secure-demo exec hardened-web -- id
kubectl -n secure-demo exec hardened-web -- sh -c 'touch /etc/x'
kubectl -n secure-demo exec hardened-web -- sh -c 'grep Cap /proc/1/status'
kubectl -n secure-demo exec hardened-web -- sh -c 'grep Seccomp /proc/1/status'
sections.title: Prove the pod is locked down
sections.output:
$ kubectl -n secure-demo exec hardened-web -- id
uid=10001 gid=10001 groups=10001

$ kubectl -n secure-demo exec hardened-web -- sh -c 'touch /etc/x'
touch: /etc/x: Read-only file system
command terminated with exit code 1

$ kubectl -n secure-demo exec hardened-web -- sh -c 'grep Cap /proc/1/status'
CapInh:	0000000000000000
CapPrm:	0000000000000000
CapEff:	0000000000000000
CapBnd:	0000000000000000
CapAmb:	0000000000000000

$ kubectl -n secure-demo exec hardened-web -- sh -c 'grep Seccomp /proc/1/status'
Seccomp:	2
Seccomp_filters:	1
sections.note: Seccomp mode 2 means a filter is active. Mode 0 would mean the process is unconfined.

sections.title: About this example: Pod Security Standards on a namespace
sections.body: Pod Security Admission is built into the API server and is configured entirely with namespace labels. This Namespace manifest enforces the `restricted` profile, so non-compliant pods are rejected, and also warns and audits against it. There are three profiles: **privileged** (unrestricted, for kube-system and CNI agents), **baseline** (blocks hostNetwork, hostPath, privileged and dangerous capabilities) and **restricted** (adds non-root, drop ALL and seccomp, the goal for app namespaces). Apply it with `kubectl apply -f`, then try to create a privileged pod in that namespace to see the rejection.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: payments
  labels:
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: restricted
    pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted
sections.title: restricted-namespace.yaml
sections.output:
$ kubectl apply -f restricted-namespace.yaml
namespace/payments created

$ kubectl -n payments run bad --image=nginx --privileged
Error from server (Forbidden): pods "bad" is forbidden: violates PodSecurity "restricted:latest": privileged (container "bad" must not set securityContext.privileged=true), allowPrivilegeEscalation != false (container "bad" must set securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation=false), unrestricted capabilities (container "bad" must set securityContext.capabilities.drop=["ALL"]), runAsNonRoot != true (pod or container "bad" must set securityContext.runAsNonRoot=true), seccompProfile (pod or container "bad" must set securityContext.seccompProfile.type to "RuntimeDefault" or "Localhost")
sections.note: Roll out safely: `enforce` rejects, `audit` annotates the audit log and `warn` prints a client warning, so label with `warn` and `audit` first, fix the warnings, and only then add `enforce`.

exercises.title: Trigger Pod Security rejection
exercises.prompt: Label a namespace with enforce=restricted and try to run a plain nginx pod.

questions.question: Which layer of the 4Cs contains securityContext settings?
questions.explain: securityContext configures runtime isolation of the container, so it belongs to the Container layer.

questions.question: What does readOnlyRootFilesystem: true require when the app must write temporary files?
options: Mounting a writable volume such as emptyDir at those paths
questions.explain: The rootfs is immutable; give the app explicit writable mounts such as emptyDir for /tmp.

questions.question: How does Pod Security Admission get configured per namespace?
questions.explain: PSA is driven by labels for the enforce, audit and warn modes.

questions.question: Which seccomp profile type is the recommended baseline?
questions.explain: RuntimeDefault applies the container runtime's default syscall filter and is required by the restricted profile.

lessons.title: RBAC in depth and ServiceAccount tokens
lessons.summary: Design least-privilege roles, aggregate them, audit access with can-i and who-can, and use short-lived projected tokens.
objectives: Spot dangerous RBAC grants such as secrets list, escalate and wildcards
Scope permissions with resourceNames and aggregated ClusterRoles
Audit access with kubectl auth can-i and use projected, bound ServiceAccount tokens

sections.title: Least privilege is a design, not a default
sections.body:
RBAC answers one question: may this subject perform this verb on this resource? It is purely additive, there are no deny rules, so the safest design starts from nothing and grants the smallest set of verbs on the smallest set of resources in the smallest scope. The usual failures are not exotic: `cluster-admin` bound to a CI account, `*` verbs, `secrets` list permission (which exposes every secret value), and the powerful verbs `escalate`, `bind` and `impersonate`, which let a holder grant themselves more.

A second, quieter risk is the ServiceAccount token. Every pod gets one by default, so a compromised pod acts with whatever RBAC that account holds. Combine narrow Roles with `automountServiceAccountToken: false` for pods that never call the API, and short-lived projected tokens for those that do.

sections.title: Dangerous permissions to hunt for
head: Permission
Why it is dangerous
Safer alternative
rows: list returns all secret data in the namespace; watch also leaks values
Grant get on named resources via resourceNames; mount only needed secrets
Shell inside any pod, including ones holding powerful tokens
Restrict to break-glass roles with time-bound bindings
A pod can mount any secret or ServiceAccount in its namespace and run privileged if PSA allows
Pair with Pod Security restricted; prefer create deployments only
Lets the holder grant permissions they do not have
Act as any user, group or ServiceAccount
Never to humans or CI; use only for audited tooling
Silently includes every future API and CRD
Reaches the kubelet API and can exec in any pod on the node
Do not grant; monitoring should use metrics endpoints

sections.title: About this example: a namespaced least-privilege Role plus an aggregated ClusterRole
sections.body: This file has two parts. The first gives a single ServiceAccount, `deployer`, the right to update exactly one Deployment and read pods and logs in the `shop` namespace. `resourceNames` pins the permission to the named object, and the RoleBinding scopes it to one namespace. There is no `delete`, no `create` and no access to secrets. The second part is an aggregated ClusterRole: its `rules` list is empty and the controller manager fills it from every ClusterRole carrying the matching label, which is how built-in `view`, `edit` and `admin` pick up CRD permissions. After applying, `kubectl get clusterrole monitoring-view -o jsonpath='{.rules[*].resources}'` shows the cert-viewer resources.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: shop
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: deployer
  namespace: shop
automountServiceAccountToken: false
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata:
  name: deployer
  namespace: shop
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["apps"]
    resources: ["deployments"]
    resourceNames: ["storefront"]
    verbs: ["get", "patch", "update"]
  - apiGroups: [""]
    resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: deployer
  namespace: shop
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: deployer
    namespace: shop
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: deployer
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: monitoring-view
aggregationRule:
  clusterRoleSelectors:
    - matchLabels:
        rbac.example.com/aggregate-to-monitoring-view: "true"
rules: []   # filled in by the controller manager
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRole
metadata:
  name: cert-viewer
  labels:
    rbac.example.com/aggregate-to-monitoring-view: "true"
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["cert-manager.io"]
    resources: ["certificates", "certificaterequests"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]
sections.title: deployer-rbac.yaml
sections.note: A RoleBinding's `roleRef` is immutable. To change it, delete and recreate the binding.

sections.title: About this example: auditing permissions with can-i and who-can
sections.body: These commands test the `deployer` account from the previous manifest, then list everything it may do. The last two lines use two community tools, `kubectl-who-can` (from Aqua) and `rakkess`, which kubectl core does not provide: they answer the reverse question, who may do X, which is what you need in a review. Compare the `yes` and `no` answers to the Role's `verbs`.

sections.code:
SA=system:serviceaccount:shop:deployer
kubectl auth can-i patch deployments/storefront -n shop --as=$SA
kubectl auth can-i delete deployments -n shop --as=$SA
kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n shop --as=$SA
kubectl auth can-i --list -n shop --as=$SA
kubectl who-can get secrets -n shop
kubectl rakkess --sa shop:deployer -n shop
sections.title: Test, list and reverse-lookup permissions
sections.output:
$ kubectl auth can-i patch deployments/storefront -n shop --as=$SA
yes
$ kubectl auth can-i delete deployments -n shop --as=$SA
no
$ kubectl auth can-i get secrets -n shop --as=$SA
no

$ kubectl auth can-i --list -n shop --as=$SA
Resources                          Non-Resource URLs   Resource Names   Verbs
pods/log                           []                  []               [get list watch]
pods                               []                  []               [get list watch]
deployments.apps                   []                  [storefront]     [get patch update]
selfsubjectaccessreviews.authorization.k8s.io  []      []               [create]

$ kubectl who-can get secrets -n shop

sections.title: About this example: projected ServiceAccount token
sections.body: Legacy tokens were long-lived Secrets that never expired. Since Kubernetes 1.22 pods receive a **bound** token: time-limited, audience-scoped, tied to the pod and removed when it dies. This Pod mounts its own projected token with a custom audience and a one-hour lifetime; the kubelet rotates it automatically at about 80 percent of its life. Check `audience`, `expirationSeconds` and the mount path `/var/run/secrets/tokens`.

sections.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: token-client
  namespace: shop
spec:
  serviceAccountName: deployer
  automountServiceAccountToken: false
  containers:
    - name: client
      image: busybox:1.36
      command: ["sleep", "3600"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: api-token
          mountPath: /var/run/secrets/tokens
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: api-token
      projected:
        sources:
          - serviceAccountToken:
              path: token
              audience: vault.example.com
              expirationSeconds: 3600
sections.title: projected-token-pod.yaml
sections.output:
$ kubectl -n shop exec token-client -- cat /var/run/secrets/tokens/token | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null
{"aud":["vault.example.com"],"exp":1763036400,"iat":1763032800,"iss":"https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local","kubernetes.io":{"namespace":"shop","pod":{"name":"token-client","uid":"c1d2e3f4-..."},"serviceaccount":{"name":"deployer","uid":"9a8b7c6d-..."}},"sub":"system:serviceaccount:shop:deployer"}
sections.note: For ad-hoc tokens use `kubectl create token deployer -n shop --duration=10m` rather than creating a Secret.

questions.question: What does an aggregated ClusterRole do?
options: Combines rules from ClusterRoles matching its label selectors
questions.explain: The controller manager copies rules from matching ClusterRoles into the aggregating role.

questions.question: Why is 'list' on secrets more dangerous than it looks?
options: It returns the full data of every secret in scope
questions.explain: List responses include secret values, so list or watch is effectively read-all.

questions.question: Which statement about projected ServiceAccount tokens is true?
options: They are bound to the pod, audience-scoped and expire
questions.explain: Bound tokens are time-limited and invalidated when the pod is deleted.

questions.question: Which command shows everything an identity may do in a namespace?
questions.explain: can-i --list enumerates allowed verbs per resource.

modules.title: Policy, secrets and supply chain
modules.summary: Admission control, secrets management, image trust and runtime detection.

lessons.title: Admission control and policy as code
lessons.summary: Enforce organisation rules at the API with ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (CEL), Kyverno and OPA Gatekeeper.
objectives: Explain mutating versus validating admission and failure policies
Write a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy and binding using CEL
Compare Kyverno and Gatekeeper policies and choose between them

sections.title: Admission control: the last gate before etcd
sections.body:
After authentication and authorization, a request passes through **admission controllers** before the object is persisted. **Mutating** webhooks may change the object (inject sidecars, set defaults); **validating** ones can only accept or reject. Built-in controllers such as Pod Security Admission cover common cases, but organisation rules like 'every image comes from our registry', 'no `latest` tag' or 'every Deployment has an owner label' need policy-as-code.

There are three practical options. **ValidatingAdmissionPolicy** (GA in Kubernetes 1.30) evaluates CEL expressions inside the API server, with no webhook to run, scale or secure. **Kyverno** is a policy engine whose policies are plain Kubernetes YAML and which can validate, mutate, generate and verify images. **OPA Gatekeeper** uses Rego in ConstraintTemplates plus Constraint objects. Choose in-tree CEL for simple rules, Kyverno for rich YAML-native policy, Gatekeeper if you already standardise on OPA.

sections.title: Policy engine comparison
head: Aspect
ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
Kyverno
OPA Gatekeeper
rows: Policy status type checking, audit action

sections.title: About this example: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy with CEL
sections.body: Two objects are needed. The policy states the rule in CEL: here every container image must come from `registry.example.com/` and may not use the `latest` tag. The binding decides where it applies and what happens on violation (`Deny`, `Warn` or `Audit`); this one denies in namespaces labelled `policy=enforced`. Check `matchConstraints` for the targeted resources and the `messageExpression`, which is what users see when they are rejected.

sections.code:
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
metadata:
  name: trusted-registry
spec:
  failurePolicy: Fail
  matchConstraints:
    resourceRules:
      - apiGroups: ["apps"]
        apiVersions: ["v1"]
        operations: ["CREATE", "UPDATE"]
        resources: ["deployments"]
  validations:
    - expression: >-
        object.spec.template.spec.containers.all(c,
          c.image.startsWith('registry.example.com/'))
      messageExpression: >-
        'images must come from registry.example.com, got: ' +
        object.spec.template.spec.containers.map(c, c.image).join(', ')
    - expression: >-
        object.spec.template.spec.containers.all(c,
          !c.image.endsWith(':latest') && c.image.contains(':'))
      message: "images must use an explicit tag other than latest"
---
apiVersion: admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1
kind: ValidatingAdmissionPolicyBinding
metadata:
  name: trusted-registry-binding
spec:
  policyName: trusted-registry
  validationActions: ["Deny"]
  matchResources:
    namespaceSelector:
      matchLabels:
        policy: enforced
sections.title: image-policy.yaml
sections.output:
$ kubectl apply -f image-policy.yaml
validatingadmissionpolicy.admissionregistration.k8s.io/trusted-registry created
validatingadmissionpolicybinding.admissionregistration.k8s.io/trusted-registry-binding created

$ kubectl label ns shop policy=enforced
namespace/shop labeled
$ kubectl -n shop create deployment web --image=nginx:latest
error: failed to create deployment: deployments.apps "web" is forbidden: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy 'trusted-registry' with binding 'trusted-registry-binding' denied request: images must come from registry.example.com, got: nginx:latest
sections.note: Start with `validationActions: ["Warn", "Audit"]` to see what would break, then switch to `Deny`.

sections.title: About this example: a Kyverno ClusterPolicy
sections.body: Kyverno policies are ordinary YAML, which makes them approachable for platform teams. This policy requires CPU and memory limits and blocks privileged containers, in `Enforce` mode. It needs Kyverno installed (`helm install kyverno kyverno/kyverno -n kyverno --create-namespace`). Look at `validationFailureAction`, the `match` block and the `pattern`, where `?*` means any non-empty value.

sections.code:
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: require-limits-no-privileged
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  background: true
  rules:
    - name: require-memory-limit
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
      validate:
        message: "Containers must set resources.limits.memory."
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - resources:
                  limits:
                    memory: "?*"
    - name: deny-privileged
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
      validate:
        message: "Privileged containers are not allowed."
        pattern:
          spec:
            containers:
              - =(securityContext):
                  =(privileged): "false"
sections.title: require-limits.yaml (requires Kyverno CRDs)
sections.output:
$ kubectl run test --image=registry.example.com/app:1.0
Error from server: admission webhook "validate.kyverno.svc-fail" denied the request:

resource Pod/default/test was blocked due to the following policies

require-limits-no-privileged:
  require-memory-limit: 'validation error: Containers must set resources.limits.memory. rule require-memory-limit failed at path /spec/containers/0/resources/limits/'
sections.note: Shown as text because it needs the Kyverno CRDs, which a plain cluster does not have.

sections.title: About this example: an OPA Gatekeeper template and constraint
sections.body: Gatekeeper splits a policy into a ConstraintTemplate, which holds the Rego logic and defines a new CRD, and a Constraint, which is an instance that picks targets and parameters. This pair requires an `owner` label on every Namespace. The `violation` rule fires when the label is missing and its `msg` is shown to the user. Install Gatekeeper first; apply the template before the constraint.

sections.code:
apiVersion: templates.gatekeeper.sh/v1
kind: ConstraintTemplate
metadata:
  name: k8srequiredlabels
spec:
  crd:
    spec:
      names:
        kind: K8sRequiredLabels
      validation:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            labels:
              type: array
              items: {type: string}
  targets:
    - target: admission.k8s.gatekeeper.sh
      rego: |
        package k8srequiredlabels
        violation[{"msg": msg}] {
          required := input.parameters.labels[_]
          not input.review.object.metadata.labels[required]
          msg := sprintf("missing required label: %v", [required])
        }
---
apiVersion: constraints.gatekeeper.sh/v1beta1
kind: K8sRequiredLabels
metadata:
  name: ns-must-have-owner
spec:
  enforcementAction: deny
  match:
    kinds:
      - apiGroups: [""]
        kinds: ["Namespace"]
  parameters:
    labels: ["owner"]
sections.title: required-labels.yaml (requires Gatekeeper)
sections.output:
$ kubectl create namespace scratch
Error from server (Forbidden): admission webhook "validation.gatekeeper.sh" denied the request: [ns-must-have-owner] missing required label: owner

$ kubectl get k8srequiredlabels ns-must-have-owner -o jsonpath='{.status.totalViolations}'
2
sections.note: Existing offenders are reported by the audit controller in `.status.violations` without being deleted.

sections.title: Webhook failure policy can take down the cluster
sections.body: A validating webhook with `failurePolicy: Fail` that matches `kube-system` or its own namespace can deadlock the cluster if the webhook pods go down: new pods, including the webhook's replacement, are rejected. Always exclude system namespaces and the policy engine's namespace, run at least 3 replicas with a PodDisruptionBudget, and set short `timeoutSeconds`. ValidatingAdmissionPolicy avoids this entire failure class because it has no webhook.

questions.question: Which admission webhook type can change the incoming object?
questions.explain: Mutating admission runs first and can modify the object; validating can only accept or reject.

lessons.title: Secrets management at scale
lessons.summary: Encrypt etcd, sync secrets from external managers, commit sealed secrets safely and rotate without downtime.
objectives: Enable and verify encryption at rest for Secrets
Choose between External Secrets, the CSI driver and Sealed Secrets
Rotate secrets and encryption keys without an outage

sections.title: Secrets are base64, not encrypted
sections.body:
A Kubernetes Secret is only base64-encoded text. By default it is stored in etcd in plain form, readable by anyone with etcd or disk-backup access and by anyone with `get` on secrets through the API. A mature secrets strategy has four parts: **encrypt etcd at rest**, **keep the source of truth outside the cluster** (a vault or cloud secret manager) and sync it in, **never commit plain Secrets to Git**, and **rotate** credentials so a leak has a short half-life.

Choose the pattern by where you want the secret to live. External Secrets Operator copies values from a manager into native Secrets. The Secrets Store CSI driver mounts them straight into the pod filesystem and can skip creating a Secret. Sealed Secrets lets you commit an encrypted form to Git that only the cluster can decrypt.

sections.title: Secrets patterns compared
head: Pattern
Source of truth
In-cluster object
Best for
Watch out for
rows: Values still visible to anyone with get secrets
Synced Secret is in etcd, so encrypt etcd too
Avoiding Secret objects, rotation by remount
Pod cannot start if the provider is unreachable
Losing the controller key loses decryptability; back it up

sections.title: About this example: encryption at rest configuration
sections.body: This is the `EncryptionConfiguration` file passed to the API server with `--encryption-provider-config`; it is a control-plane file, not something you `kubectl apply`, so it is shown as text. The first provider in each list is used for writing and all are tried for reading. Put `aescbc` or `secretbox` before `identity`, and for production prefer a `kms` v2 provider, which keeps the key outside the cluster. After enabling, existing secrets stay plaintext until rewritten with the command below.

sections.code:
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources:
      - secrets
    providers:
      - aescbc:
          keys:
            - name: key-2026-11
              secret: <base64 of 32 random bytes>
      - identity: {}
# KMS v2 alternative (key lives in the cloud KMS/HSM, not on the control plane):
#   - kms:
#       apiVersion: v2
#       name: cloud-kms
#       endpoint: unix:///var/run/kms/socket.sock
#       timeout: 3s
sections.title: /etc/kubernetes/enc/encryption-config.yaml
sections.output:
# Re-encrypt every existing secret after enabling or rotating the key
$ kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -
secret/db-creds replaced
secret/api-token replaced

# Verify on the control plane: ciphertext shows the provider prefix
$ ETCDCTL_API=3 etcdctl get /registry/secrets/shop/db-creds | hexdump -C | head -3
00000000  2f 72 65 67 69 73 74 72  79 2f 73 65 63 72 65 74  |/registry/secret|
00000010  73 2f 73 68 6f 70 2f 64  62 2d 63 72 65 64 73 0a  |s/shop/db-creds.|
00000020  6b 38 73 3a 65 6e 63 3a  61 65 73 63 62 63 3a 76  |k8s:enc:aescbc:v|
sections.note: Output beginning `k8s:enc:aescbc:v1:` proves encryption. Plain JSON starting with `{` or `k8s\x00` means unencrypted.

sections.title: About this example: External Secrets Operator
sections.body: Two manifests make the sync work. The `ClusterSecretStore` tells the operator how to authenticate to an external manager (here AWS Secrets Manager using IRSA, an IAM role bound to a ServiceAccount, so no static keys). The `ExternalSecret` names the keys to fetch, the target Secret to create and the `refreshInterval`; rotating the value in the manager updates the Secret within that interval. Needs the operator CRDs, so shown as text.

sections.code:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata:
  name: aws-secrets
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: eu-west-1
      auth:
        jwt:
          serviceAccountRef:
            name: eso-sa
            namespace: external-secrets
---
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: db-creds
  namespace: shop
spec:
  refreshInterval: 15m
  secretStoreRef:
    kind: ClusterSecretStore
    name: aws-secrets
  target:
    name: db-creds
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
    - secretKey: password
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/shop/db
        property: password
sections.title: external-secret.yaml (requires External Secrets Operator)
sections.output:
$ kubectl -n shop get externalsecret db-creds
NAME       STORE         REFRESH INTERVAL   STATUS         READY
db-creds   aws-secrets   15m                SecretSynced   True
sections.note: `STATUS SecretSynced` and `READY True` mean the target Secret exists and matches the source.

sections.title: About this example: Sealed Secrets workflow
sections.body: The `kubeseal` CLI encrypts a Secret with the controller's public key, producing a `SealedSecret` that is safe to commit. Only the controller in the target cluster can decrypt it, and by default the ciphertext is bound to the name and namespace, so it cannot be replayed elsewhere. Run the commands from a workstation with cluster access; note that the generated file contains only `encryptedData`.

sections.code:
kubectl create secret generic db-creds -n shop \
  --from-literal=password='S3cr3t!' --dry-run=client -o yaml \
  | kubeseal --controller-name sealed-secrets --controller-namespace kube-system -o yaml > db-creds-sealed.yaml
cat db-creds-sealed.yaml
kubectl apply -f db-creds-sealed.yaml
kubectl -n shop get secret db-creds
sections.title: Seal a secret and apply it
sections.output:
$ cat db-creds-sealed.yaml
apiVersion: bitnami.com/v1alpha1
kind: SealedSecret
metadata:
  name: db-creds
  namespace: shop
spec:
  encryptedData:
    password: AgBy8hCi7F2...truncated...Qk9=
  template:
    metadata:
      name: db-creds
      namespace: shop

$ kubectl apply -f db-creds-sealed.yaml
sealedsecret.bitnami.com/db-creds created
$ kubectl -n shop get secret db-creds
NAME       TYPE     DATA   AGE
db-creds   Opaque   1      4s
sections.note: Back up the controller key (`kubectl get secret -n kube-system -l sealedsecrets.bitnami.com/sealed-secrets-key`) and rotate it; sealing keys renew every 30 days by default.

sections.title: Rotation checklist
sections.body: Rotate in this order so nothing breaks: add the new credential at the source, let ExternalSecret or CSI refresh it, then restart pods that read it from environment variables (they never see updates; mounted files do, after the kubelet sync delay). Prefer mounting secrets as files over env vars, use a tool such as Reloader to roll Deployments on change, and revoke the old credential only after all pods run with the new one. Rotate the encryption key by adding a new key first in the list, restarting API servers, rewriting all secrets, then removing the old key.

questions.question: What is the main weakness of a default Kubernetes Secret?
options: It is encrypted with a weak cipher
It is only base64-encoded and stored unencrypted in etcd
questions.explain: Without encryption at rest, secret data sits in etcd in plain form.

questions.question: In an EncryptionConfiguration, which provider writes new data?
questions.explain: The first provider encrypts writes; all listed providers are tried for reads.

questions.question: Why are pods using secrets as env vars not updated on rotation?
options: Env vars are fixed at container start
questions.explain: Environment variables are set when the container starts; mounted files are refreshed by the kubelet.

questions.question: What does a SealedSecret protect against?
questions.explain: It is encrypted so only the in-cluster controller can decrypt it, making it safe to store in Git.

lessons.title: Supply chain, runtime detection and audit
lessons.summary: Scan, build SBOMs, sign images with cosign, verify at admission and detect abuse with Falco and API audit logs.
objectives: Generate an SBOM, scan an image and sign it by digest with cosign
Configure API audit policy and runtime detection rules

sections.title: Trust what you run: the software supply chain
sections.body:
A container image is code from many authors: your application, base image, OS packages and language dependencies. Supply-chain security answers three questions about each image: **what is in it** (SBOM), **is it vulnerable** (scanning) and **who built it and was it tampered with** (signatures and provenance). The cluster then enforces the answers at admission time, so an unsigned or high-severity image never starts.

Runtime protection is the last layer. Even a clean, signed image can be exploited through a zero-day, so you also want detection of unexpected behaviour (a shell spawned in a web container, a write to `/etc`) and a Kubernetes audit log that records who changed what in the API.

sections.title: Supply-chain controls and where they run
head: Control
Tool examples
Runs in
Result
rows: SPDX or CycloneDX file listing every package
CI and on a schedule in the registry
CVE list with severity; fail build on CRITICAL
cosign (keyless via OIDC or key pair)
Signature and attestation stored next to the image in the registry
Unsigned or untrusted images rejected; tags rewritten to digests
Alerts on shell in container, sensitive file read, unexpected egress
JSON events for every API request, shipped to a SIEM

sections.title: About this example: sign, attest and scan in CI
sections.body: This is the sequence a CI job runs after building and pushing an image. It scans with Trivy and fails on HIGH or CRITICAL findings, generates a CycloneDX SBOM, then signs the image **by digest** (never by tag, which can be moved) and attaches the SBOM as a signed attestation. In GitHub Actions or GitLab, keyless signing uses the job's OIDC identity, so no private key is stored. Notice the `@sha256:` reference in each command.

sections.code:
IMAGE=registry.example.com/shop/api
DIGEST=$(crane digest $IMAGE:1.4.2)
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 $IMAGE@$DIGEST
trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.cdx.json $IMAGE@$DIGEST
cosign sign --yes $IMAGE@$DIGEST
cosign attest --yes --type cyclonedx --predicate sbom.cdx.json $IMAGE@$DIGEST
cosign verify $IMAGE@$DIGEST \
  --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/example/shop/.*' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
sections.title: CI supply-chain steps
sections.output:
$ trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 registry.example.com/shop/api@sha256:9f2c...
registry.example.com/shop/api (debian 12.7)
Total: 0 (HIGH: 0, CRITICAL: 0)

$ cosign sign --yes registry.example.com/shop/api@sha256:9f2c...
Generating ephemeral keys...
Retrieving signed certificate...
tlog entry created with index: 128440217
Pushing signature to: registry.example.com/shop/api

$ cosign verify registry.example.com/shop/api@sha256:9f2c... --certificate-identity-regexp '...' --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
Verification for registry.example.com/shop/api@sha256:9f2c... --
The following checks were performed on each of these signatures:
  - The cosign claims were validated
  - Existence of the claims in the transparency log was verified offline
  - The code-signing certificate was verified using trusted certificate authority certificates
sections.note: If `trivy` exits 1 the pipeline stops before signing, so only scanned images ever get a signature.

sections.title: About this example: verify signatures at admission with Kyverno
sections.body: This ClusterPolicy makes the cluster reject any Pod image from `registry.example.com/shop/*` that lacks a valid cosign signature from your CI identity. `mutateDigest: true` rewrites the tag to the immutable digest, so what was verified is exactly what runs. The `keyless` block pins both the OIDC issuer and the subject, which prevents anyone else's Sigstore identity from passing. It needs Kyverno installed, so it is shown as text.

sections.code:
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata:
  name: verify-image-signatures
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  webhookTimeoutSeconds: 30
  rules:
    - name: check-cosign
      match:
        any:
          - resources:
              kinds: ["Pod"]
      verifyImages:
        - imageReferences:
            - "registry.example.com/shop/*"
          mutateDigest: true
          verifyDigest: true
          required: true
          attestors:
            - entries:
                - keyless:
                    issuer: https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
                    subject: https://github.com/example/shop/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main
                    rekor:
                      url: https://rekor.sigstore.dev
sections.title: verify-images.yaml (requires Kyverno)
sections.output:
$ kubectl -n shop run rogue --image=registry.example.com/shop/api:unsigned
Error from server: admission webhook "mutate.kyverno.svc-fail" denied the request:

resource Pod/shop/rogue was blocked due to the following policies

verify-image-signatures:
  check-cosign: 'failed to verify image registry.example.com/shop/api:unsigned: .attestors[0].entries[0].keyless: no signatures found'

sections.title: About this example: API audit policy and runtime detection rule
sections.body: The first part is a kube-apiserver audit policy (passed with `--audit-policy-file`): it logs secret access at `Metadata` level so values never reach the log, records full request and response for RBAC changes, and drops noisy read-only health calls. The second part is a Falco rule that alerts when a shell starts inside a container. Both are control-plane or node configuration, not applicable manifests, so they are text. Rules are evaluated top to bottom and the first match wins.

sections.code:
# --- /etc/kubernetes/audit-policy.yaml ---
apiVersion: audit.k8s.io/v1
kind: Policy
omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]
rules:
  - level: None
    nonResourceURLs: ["/healthz*", "/livez*", "/readyz*"]
  - level: Metadata          # who read secrets, never the values
    resources:
      - group: ""
        resources: ["secrets", "configmaps"]
  - level: RequestResponse   # full detail for permission changes
    resources:
      - group: "rbac.authorization.k8s.io"
        resources: ["roles", "rolebindings", "clusterroles", "clusterrolebindings"]
  - level: Request
    verbs: ["create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
  - level: Metadata

# --- Falco rule ---
- rule: Shell in container
  desc: A shell was started inside a container
  condition: >
    evt.type = execve and evt.dir = < and container.id != host
    and proc.name in (bash, sh, zsh)
  output: >
    Shell in container (user=%user.name pod=%k8s.pod.name ns=%k8s.ns.name
    cmd=%proc.cmdline image=%container.image.repository)
  priority: WARNING
  tags: [container, shell, mitre_execution]
sections.title: audit-policy.yaml and falco rule
sections.output:
# Sample audit log line (JSON, one per line, truncated)
{"kind":"Event","level":"RequestResponse","verb":"create","user":{"username":"alice@example.com","groups":["devs"]},"objectRef":{"resource":"clusterrolebindings","name":"temp-admin"},"responseStatus":{"code":201},"requestReceivedTimestamp":"2026-11-13T10:22:41Z"}

# Sample Falco alert
10:24:03.118: Warning Shell in container (user=root pod=api-7d9c8b6f5-abcde ns=shop cmd=sh -c id image=registry.example.com/shop/api)

sections.title: Defence in depth recap
sections.body: No single control is enough: scanning finds known flaws, signing proves origin, admission enforces both, Pod Security and securityContext limit blast radius, RBAC limits what a stolen token can do and audit logs plus runtime detection tell you when something slips through. Review the whole chain with the exercise list from each lesson in this course and with the production checklist.

questions.question: Why sign an image by digest and not by tag?
options: A tag can be moved to a different image, a digest cannot
Cosign only supports digests for speed
Tags are not allowed in registries
questions.explain: Digests are immutable content addresses; tags are mutable pointers.

questions.question: What does an SBOM provide?
options: A list of the components inside an image
questions.explain: A software bill of materials lists packages and versions for vulnerability matching and audits.

questions.question: At which audit level is a secret read logged without exposing the value?
questions.explain: Metadata logs who and what, but not request or response bodies.

questions.question: What does Kyverno verifyImages with mutateDigest do?
options: Verifies signatures and rewrites the tag to the verified digest
questions.explain: It enforces signature checks and pins the image reference to the exact verified digest.
